claims.claim: Stereotyped neighbor relationships within a bundle can arise from differential adhesion.
claims.source: These studies led to two major principles, which are further supported by the work described here: first, that neurites can exhibit stereotyped neighbor relationships within a bundle and, second, that these relationships can arise from differential adhesion.
claims.evidence: Synthesis of findings from multiple studies

claims.claim: Multiple adhesion molecules can act in concert to specify distinct relationships among many neurites, in a pattern that is more complex than 1:1 pairing or inside:outside relationships.
claims.source: Importantly, our study introduces a third principle – that multiple adhesion molecules can act in concert to specify distinct relationships among many neurites, in a pattern that is more complex than the 1:1 pairing of G and P axons or the inside:outside relationship of L and R neurites.
claims.evidence: Inference from the current study's findings

claims.claim: Bundle order does not reflect the developmental order of neurite outgrowth in C. elegans.
claims.source: One trivial explanation would be that bundle order reflects the developmental order of neurite outgrowth, with the oldest neurite – typically the pioneer axon or dendrite – in the center, and the youngest neurites on the periphery. However, this is not the case in C. elegans, the only organism in which the birth order and neurite position of every neuron is known.
claims.evidence: Statement based on knowledge of C. elegans development

claims.claim: VD motor neurons are born post-embryonically and extend axons along the ventral nerve cord after the nerve cord is established, yet their axons insinuate deeply into the ventral nerve cord to adhere closely to the DD motor neurons.
claims.source: As an example, the VD motor neurons are born post-embryonically and extend axons along the ventral nerve cord after the nerve cord is established, yet their axons insinuate deeply into the ventral nerve cord to adhere closely to the DD motor neurons, a functionally similar set of motoneurons that are born much earlier and lie at the center of the ventral nerve cord (White et al., 1976; White et al., 1986).
claims.evidence: Supported by citations to White et al., 1976 and White et al., 1986

claims.claim: Neurites 'choose' their neighbors within a bundle, possibly with functional consequences.
claims.source: This and similar examples suggest that neurites 'choose' their neighbors within a bundle, possibly with functional consequences.
claims.evidence: Inference from observations in C. elegans

claims.claim: The dendrites of gonadotropin-releasing hormone neurons are intertwined in bundles, and this arrangement has been proposed to help synchronize hormone release.
claims.source: For example, the dendrites of gonadotropin-releasing hormone neurons are intertwined in bundles, and this arrangement has been proposed to help synchronize hormone release (Campbell et al., 2009).
claims.evidence: Supported by citation to Campbell et al., 2009

claims.claim: Neuropeptide-releasing neurons in Drosophila that serve as circadian pacemakers undergo daily changes in axon fasciculation, driven by cycling expression levels of the NCAM adhesion molecule FAS2.
claims.source: In a possibly related example, neuropeptide-releasing neurons in Drosophila that serve as circadian pacemakers undergo daily changes in axon fasciculation, driven by cycling expression levels of the NCAM adhesion molecule FAS2 (Fernández et al., 2008; Sivachenko et al., 2013).
claims.evidence: Supported by citations to Fernández et al., 2008 and Sivachenko et al., 2013

claims.claim: Genetically manipulating FAS2 expression to force constitutive defasciculation leads to changes in circadian behavior.
claims.source: Interestingly, genetically manipulating FAS2 expression to force constitutive defasciculation leads to changes in circadian behavior, suggesting that fasciculation may indeed affect neuronal activity (Sivachenko et al., 2013).
claims.evidence: Supported by citation to Sivachenko et al., 2013

claims.source: Consistent with this notion, Ferenczi et al. used an engineering approach to optogenetically manipulate ion flow in hippocampal and cortical axons and observed a 'bystander' effect on the membrane current of neighboring axons, independent of synaptic transmission (Ferenczi et al., 2016).
claims.evidence: Supported by citation to Ferenczi et al., 2016

claims.claim: In wild-type Drosophila, a short pulse of odor-induced activity in one olfactory dendrite inhibited tonic firing of its bundled neighbor, independently of chemical or electrical synapses.
claims.source: Remarkably, in wild-type Drosophila, Carlson and colleagues demonstrated similar ephaptic effects between bundled olfactory dendrites (Su et al., 2012): a short pulse of odor-induced activity in one of these dendrites inhibited tonic firing of its bundled neighbor, independently of chemical or electrical synapses.
claims.evidence: Supported by citation to Su et al., 2012

claims.claim: Ephaptic effects between bundled olfactory dendrites in Drosophila can alter behavioral responses.
claims.source: Importantly, they showed that this ephaptic effect could even alter behavioral responses.
claims.evidence: Supported by reference to Su et al., 2012 study

claims.claim: Amphid sensilla in other nematode species such as Acrobeles complexus, Strongyloides stercoralis, and Haemonchus contortus exhibit well-ordered bundles, albeit with configurations that are different from each other and from C. elegans.
claims.source: Interestingly, amphid sensilla in other nematode species such as Acrobeles complexus, Strongyloides stercoralis, and Haemonchus contortus also exhibit well-ordered bundles, albeit with configurations that are different from each other and from C. elegans (Bumbarger et al., 2009).
claims.evidence: Supported by citation to Bumbarger et al., 2009

claims.claim: The diversity of amphid bundle structures in different nematode species may have arisen partly through altered expression of a small number of CAMs.
claims.source: It is interesting to speculate whether this diversity of structures may have arisen partly through altered expression of a small number of CAMs.
claims.evidence: Speculative interpretation based on the study's findings

results.result: The authors developed a semi-automated imaging and quantification pipeline to measure dendrite order in live C. elegans larvae and adults. Amphid dendrites remain tightly fasciculated throughout larval development, with bundle width approximately doubling from 0.88 μm at 24 hr to 1.51 μm at 72 hr.
results.evaluation: Claims C17-C22 provide quantitative measurements with clear sample sizes and standard deviations. The resolution limits are acknowledged (C17-C18), and the doubling in bundle width (C23) is presented as speculation rather than established fact. The methodological approach is well-documented with appropriate technical controls.

results.result: Amphid dendrites exhibit stereotyped order along the bundle length, with a reproducible switch point where AFD occupies the middle position near the nose tip and ASE takes over more posteriorly. This order is maintained but becomes noisier with age. The switch point correlates with where the socket glial cell joins the bundle but not with the AUA dendrite ending.
results.evaluation: Claims C24-C30 are supported by quantitative data from multiple time points (n=20 per timepoint) and confirmed with a different set of neurons (C30). The correlation analysis (C31-C32) provides mechanistic insight, though causation is not established. Statistical validation using permutation tests strengthens these observations.

results.result: Dendrite order does not require sensory cilia, proper ciliary arrangement, or interactions with sheath glia. Loss of cilia (daf-19; daf-12 mutants), disorganized cilia (mec-8 mutants), or ablation of sheath glia all preserve normal dendrite fasciculation and order.
results.evaluation: Claims C33-C42 are supported by experiments in three different genetic backgrounds with appropriate controls (n=18-20 per condition). The inference that activity is not required (C34) is logical given that cilia are required for sensory function. However, the glia ablation experiment (C40-C41) only tests maintenance after initial development, not establishment, which is appropriately noted.

results.result: A candidate screen of 20 cell adhesion molecules identified eight CAMs (dig-1, ptp-3, sax-7, vab-1, sax-3, cdh-4, unc-40, nrx-1) that cause defasciculation defects when mutated, though with low penetrance (<25%), suggesting redundancy among CAMs in maintaining fasciculation.
results.evaluation: Claims C45-C48 provide quantitative penetrance data from the dye-filling screen (n=50 per genotype). The inference of redundancy (C49) is reasonable given the low penetrance. However, the screen is limited to candidate genes rather than being genome-wide, and some mutants with defasciculation also have pleiotropic defects that complicate interpretation.

results.result: Loss of the Fat-like cadherin CDH-4 causes nearly complete randomization of dendrite order (16/21 animals) despite dendrites remaining well-fasciculated. This phenotype is present in young larvae and does not result from cell body mispositioning, indicating CDH-4 plays an essential role in specifying dendrite order.
results.evaluation: Claims C54-C57 are supported by quantitative analysis with statistical validation (permutation tests). The temporal analysis (C58) and cell body positioning control (C59) strengthen the conclusion. However, the sample size is modest (n=16-21), and the mechanism by which CDH-4 specifies order remains unclear. The conclusion (C60) appropriately distinguishes between fasciculation and ordering functions.

results.result: PTP-3/LAR and SAX-7/L1CAM are required to establish and maintain dendrite order. In young larvae, loss of either gene produces altered non-random order (shifted switch point in ptp-3; ASE/AWC equiprobable in sax-7), which progressively deteriorates to random order in adults. Double mutants show enhanced defects, and the phenotypes are specific to particular isoforms.
results.evaluation: Claims C65-C74 provide detailed temporal analysis across three developmental stages with appropriate sample sizes (n=20-24). The isoform specificity (C69) and cell body positioning controls (C70) strengthen the conclusions. The inference that these CAMs establish and maintain order (C75-C76) is well-supported by the temporal progression. However, the molecular mechanism remains unclear, and the observation of non-random intermediate states (C77) is intriguing but not fully explained.

results.result: Expression analysis using promoter-reporter constructs shows differential expression of ptp-3b (highest in AWB and ASE) and sax-7S (consistently in AWC, ASE, ASK) among amphid neurons, consistent with a model where differential CAM expression determines neighbor preferences through adhesion or signaling.
results.evaluation: Claims C79-C80 describe expression patterns, but these are based on synthetic promoter constructs that may not fully recapitulate endogenous expression. The consistency with differential adhesion models (C81) is speculative and not directly tested. While the expression patterns are suggestive, they do not prove the mechanism, and protein-level expression or localization data would strengthen this result.

results.result: Loss of sax-7 or ptp-3 causes weakly-penetrant defasciculation (<15% of animals) but highly-penetrant changes in dendrite order, with order becoming increasingly random over time and correlating with increased defasciculation.
results.evaluation: Claims C82-C85 summarize the key findings from the detailed temporal analysis. The distinction between fasciculation and ordering phenotypes is well-supported by the data, though the mechanistic link between progressive defasciculation and loss of order is correlative rather than causal. The sample sizes and statistical analyses support these conclusions.

results.result: Misexpression of SAX-7 in additional neurons at higher levels causes subtle but reproducible changes in dendrite order, shifting the switch point posteriorly, suggesting SAX-7 plays an instructive role in specifying dendrite arrangement, possibly through differential adhesion.
results.evaluation: Claim C86 describes reproducible changes with appropriate sample sizes (n=16-18). However, the changes are subtle, and the conclusion that SAX-7 is instructive (C87) is somewhat speculative. The experiment demonstrates that altering SAX-7 expression can change order, but does not definitively prove the mechanism is through differential adhesion versus signaling or other functions. Additional experiments would strengthen this conclusion.

results.result: The authors conclude that amphid dendrites are ordered within bundles through multiple CAMs expressed by neurons rather than through structures at dendrite endings. Loss of CDH-4 randomizes order, while loss or misexpression of PTP-3/SAX-7 produces altered non-random arrangements, suggesting CAM expression patterns determine dendrite arrangement.
results.evaluation: Claims C88-C94 accurately summarize the main findings. The negative results with cilia and glia (C89) and positive results with CAMs (C90-C93) are well-supported. The overall model (C94) is consistent with the data, though the precise molecular mechanisms remain to be determined. The work establishes principles but leaves mechanistic details for future investigation.

results.result: The authors place their work in context of prior studies showing that neurites can exhibit stereotyped neighbor relationships within bundles (grasshopper G-P axons, Drosophila visual system), and that these relationships can arise from differential adhesion. They propose a third principle: multiple adhesion molecules can specify complex patterns among many neurites.
results.evaluation: Claims C95-C102 accurately cite prior work establishing principles of bundle organization and differential adhesion. The proposed third principle (C103) is a reasonable inference from the current data showing that multiple CAMs (CDH-4, PTP-3, SAX-7) act together to specify order among multiple dendrites. This represents a conceptual advance over simpler 1:1 or inside:outside relationships.

results.result: Bundle order in C. elegans does not simply reflect developmental birth order or outgrowth sequence. For example, VD motor neurons born post-embryonically insinuate into the ventral nerve cord to adhere to earlier-born DD neurons, suggesting neurites actively choose neighbors with possible functional consequences.
results.evaluation: Claims C104-C105 are supported by established knowledge of C. elegans development and appropriate citations. The inference that neurites choose neighbors (C106) is reasonable but speculative regarding functional consequences. This discussion point contextualizes the findings but does not present new experimental data.

results.result: The authors discuss potential functional consequences of bundle organization, including synchronization of hormone release, circadian regulation of fasciculation, and ephaptic coupling between bundled neurites that can affect activity and behavior, as demonstrated in other systems.
results.evaluation: Claims C107-C112 accurately cite prior work from other systems showing functional consequences of bundle organization. These are appropriately presented as discussion points to motivate future work rather than as findings of the current study. The citations support the plausibility of functional consequences, though these remain to be tested in the amphid system.

results.result: Amphid bundles in other nematode species (Acrobeles complexus, Strongyloides stercoralis, Haemonchus contortus) exhibit well-ordered but different configurations from C. elegans, potentially arising from altered CAM expression.
results.evaluation: Claim C113 is supported by appropriate citation. Claim C114 is explicitly speculative and appropriately presented as such. This discussion point suggests evolutionary implications but does not present new data. The speculation is reasonable given the findings but remains untested.
